title: Born at Gujranwala, 1780
hookLine: smallpox left the boy with one eye, and tradition says he laughed about it

cards: A small boy lies in a fevered room in Gujranwala, a town in the Punjab plains. The sickness is smallpox. He lives, but the histories say it leaves its marks: a scarred face, and the sight gone from one eye.
Plenty of children would carry that like a weight. Tradition remembers this one differently. The boy grows up, becomes a ruler, and when people stare at the face, he laughs.
The scars stay. The laughter stays too.

teach.b: Gujranwala was the home ground of the Sukerchakia misl, the band led by the boy's father, Maha Singh. So this child was born into the misl world this path has just walked through.
Nobody in that room could have known he would one day pull those bands together under one rule. Then the sickness.
The sources agree on the marks it left, and they don't pretend he was handsome; some accounts describe him as short and plain, with a pitted face. What they remember is how he carried it.

teach.h: ONE EYE TO SEE ALL ALIKE.
teach.b: Now the story people love to tell. Tradition says someone once asked the Maharaja why God had given him only one eye.

His answer, as the story goes: with one eye he sees everyone the same way, Hindu, Muslim and Sikh, all with a single look. It may be a story polished by years of retelling; keep it as tradition. But see what it does.
It takes a loss and turns it into a joke, and the joke into a promise about how he'll rule. That promise has roots in the Guru Granth Sahib.
In Sohila, the prayer Sikhs say at bedtime, Guru Nanak says that one light is within everyone, and the light in all is the light of the One.
Whether or not he ever said the line about the eye, it's a very Sikh joke: the eye is less, and the seeing is more.

how: Sikhs remember Maharaja Ranjit Singh in histories, songs and stories, and the tale of his one eye is retold as a sign that he looked on people of every faith alike.

games.why: tradition says he laughed and said that with one eye he sees Hindu, Muslim and Sikh the same way. the loss became a joke, and the joke a promise.

practice: Bring to mind one thing about yourself you'd rather people didn't notice, a scar, a habit, a laugh that's too loud, and look at it the way a kind friend would. Is there anything funny in it, anything it's taught you?
Let one small smile come, with yourself rather than at yourself, and if you pray, say Waheguru on the breath out.
